speechtext:
In view of the request made yesterday and the interest that has been shown by a great many members of the house, and also because of the fact there may be some delay before we reach orders of the day, I should like to make the report I promised yesterday. It is in the form of a message received by the Minister of Labour at 12.25 p.m. today containing a joint statement issued by the railways and the unions regarding the railway dispute. This was reported as being given to the press by the parties within the next hour. I shall quote it as follows:
Although the meeting held on Tuesday, May 8th, at the request of the Minister of Labour made no progress towards a settlement of the dispute the railways and the 15 non-operating unions, having in mind their responsibility for maintaining uninterrupted railway service to the Canadian public, have arranged for a further meeting tomorrow for the purpose of entering into an agreement implementing the terms of settlement recommended by the board of conciliation notwithstanding that both parties disagree with some of the principles underlying that report.
I have nothing to add, except to say that, on behalf of the Department of Labour, the Canadian government and, I think, every hon. member of this house I express congratulations and appreciation to the two parties to this pending settlement for their patience, perseverance and patriotism. I say patriotism advisedly because I know that, in all the consideration of this dispute by the two parties, the public welfare and the national interest have been paramount as they always must be in free collective bargaining in Canada.
Commendation is due to the board of conciliation for being successful during the long hearings last winter in finding ground on which both sides can now get together.

speechtext:
Government notices of motions. Before hon. members rise may I take up the point where I left off yesterday. I quote from Hansard at page 3726, where I said:
Now, I offered earlier to delay the judgment in this case until tomorrow. Hon. members have indicated that they wanted to have a ruling now. I have given my ruling and I think we have had a discussion of sufficient length. I will say this to hon. members. If after reading Hansard tomorrow morning and after consulting with the Clerk there is any reason why something should be done in order to remove the resolution from the order paper, I will see to it that that action is taken. But if, on the other hand, after carefully reading all the arguments that have been put forward and all the authorities that have been cited and after discussing the matter fully with the Clerk and his assistants I have to come to the same conclusion that the matter may still be considered by the house, then it will be on the order paper tomorrow.
Now, immediately after the termination of the discussion yesterday I asked the Clerk to prepare a written opinion on the matter. As hon. members know, I left the chair at some time after four o'clock yesterday afternoon, and I must admit that I did not have as much time as I would have liked to consider the points that have been raised. There are many witnesses who can testify as to where I was last evening, and I want to say that, like all those who were there, I found the evening most enjoyable. This morning it was my pleasure and privilege to meet two groups, one of students and another of members of a very well known service club in Montreal, and I received other persons. Therefore, I have not had very much time, but the Clerk, fortunately for us, has spent most of his time since four o'clock yesterday afternoon on the matter, and he gave to me around one o'clock this afternoon the following opinion:
Dear Mr. Speaker:
With reference to the proceedings on the government notice of motion respecting the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Corporation, the following observations are submitted for your consideration.
On Tuesday, May 8, the new notice was received from the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce, and as is usual in every case, I carefully considered the matter before I authorized the printing of the new notice at the back of the Votes and Proceedings.
The new measure contained provisions not provided for in the original resolution and since it would not be in order, without unanimous consent, to propose the new provisions as amendments to the initial resolution in committee of the whole, the second resolution, in my opinion, presented a new proposition.
In regard to the moving of amendments to a money resolution, May's fifteenth edition, page 750, states:

"Accordingly, in this case the committee's power of amendment is strictly limited to reduction of the demand thereby made. This limitation on the power of proposing amendments applies equally to ministers of the crown as to unofficial members"-
There is no rule that I know of which prohibits the presentation of two money resolutions relating to the same subject and containing different provisions. In the second session of 1945, two resolutions relating to the Senate and House of Commons Act were on the order paper at the same time. The resolution, presented secondly, was adopted in committee of the whole and, subsequently, the order for the consideration of the one first presented was discharged. (See Journals, 1945, second session, p. 481).
There are several cases where money resolutions have been amended by means of supplementary resolutions before the consideration of the initial resolution was undertaken in committee of the whole. For examples of such amendments see Journals, 1926-7, pp. 213-15; also 1932-3, p. 431; also 1945, second session, p. 370; also 1951, first session, p. 322. On the other hand, an extensive search of the Journals has failed to produce a precedent wherein a supplementary resolution has been introduced to amend a resolution which had been partially considered in committee of the whole.
It is my contention that a money resolution is an integral and inseparable part of a money bill and that the stages of such bills include any necessary financial resolutions. May's fifteenth edition, page 503, in a paragraph entitled "Synopsis of Stages of a Bill", states that "such stages may be taken to include the stages of any necessary financial resolution".
At page 487 of the same authority, it is also stated:
"A certain class of bills, the main object of which is the expenditure of money or the imposition of taxation, must, in accordance with the requirements of the standing orders regarding charges on the people, originate in committee of the whole house".
Beauchesne's third edition, citation 433, in part, reads as follows:
"All bills providing for the payment of salaries or for any expenditure whatever out of the public funds of the dominion must be first considered as resolutions in committee of the whole" . . .
Consequently, in my opinion, a money resolution is subject to the principle which permits the presentation of two or more bills relating to the same object, provided that when a decision is rendered upon one proposal, the other measure cannot be proceeded with.
In the fifteenth edition of May at page 499, it is stated:
"There is no rule or custom which restrains the presentation of two or more bills relating to the same subject, and containing similar provisions. But if a decision of the house has already been taken on one such bill, for example, if the bill has been given or refused a second reading, the other is not proceeded with if it contains substantially the same provisions" . . .
Bourinot at page 548 of his fourth edition states:
"Whilst a bill is still pending, and until it is completely disposed of, there is nothing whatever to prevent another bill for the same object being introduced" . . . No objection can be raised to the introduction of a bill into the House of Commons on the ground of there being a similar bill already before the house.
It is the rejection and not the pendency of a bill that creates a difficulty as to the ulterior proceedings" . . .
Business of the House
The memorandum concludes:
In view of the foregoing, it is my duty to recommend that the notice of the proposed new resolution be printed as a government notice of motion on Thursday's order paper.
Respectfully submitted,
Leon J. Raymond,
Clerk of the House.

I assume this time that hon. members opposite have read both resolutions, a position which they apparently did not enjoy yesterday. Hence I will not proceed further with the reading of the resolution. However, I will say that a comparison of the two resolutions indicates that they are in exactly the same terms, paragraph by paragraph, with the addition of only one new paragraph in the new resolution. We are therefore being asked to make the same decision as was made on an earlier question, and that is this: Does this house desire that the Speaker leave the chair so that these terms may be referred to the committee of the whole for discussion? Those of us who think that the Speaker should not leave the chair for that purpose and that we should not proceed one day, one hour, one minute or one inch with the government's proposal will be faced with the necessity of making the same decision as we made and on which we voted on an earlier occasion. Those opposite who think that the proposal should be proceeded with and should be proceeded with as soon as possible will be faced with the same question for decision and it is extremely likely that they will be required once again to vote on that question. How then could it be more clear that the same question is going to be before the house again for decision if the motion now standing on the order paper is allowed to stand there and be submitted to the house for its decision in due course?
If Your Honour-as you did-places considerable reliance on Campion with respect to the rule of anticipation and the application of the rule, then I submit on that ground alone, even if the others did not exist, it is clearly out of order for this resolution to remain on the order paper because Campion says that the principle is one which forbids the same question being raised twice in the same session. Hence there are three points, as I see it. The way for the government to deal with the problem is not to introduce an amendment, because that procedure is out of order on the basis of the authority of May; and not to introduce some resolution which raises the same question-for even although something additional may be added to it, there is still the same question for decision-because that offends the rule against anticipation. In short. I submit that
{Mr. Tucker.]

Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to make it clear that in arguing with the memorandum that Your Honour has read, I am, with great respect, arguing with you rather than with our esteemed friend who prepared the memorandum for you. I am also in the fortunate position, I believe, of being able to address my remarks to the statements which you made in reading from that memorandum. In other words, my homework since yesterday has been along parallel lines. If I may say so, I believe I am in a position to answer all of the points that you made a few minutes ago. I may add, Mr. Speaker, that I will be calling some rather eminent authorities, not only the books to which we usually refer, but I shall also quote either the words or the actions of Right Hon. James Ilsley, Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, Hon. Walter Harris and Hon. Louis Rene Beaudoin, than whom one could hardly find better authorities.
You said earlier, Mr. Speaker, that this new motion was regarded as containing new matter and therefore as a new motion that it was in a category sufficiently different from the first one that it was proper to place it on the order paper. I am not now arguing with the fact it is on the order paper because that decision has been made, and it is there. What I am contending on this point of order is that Your Honour should not put the question to the house. The fact of the matter is that the new motion contains all that was in the previous motion plus additional matter, which makes it, along the lines of a precedent to which 1 will refer in a moment, substantially the same as the one already on the order paper.
Your Honour has quoted the authorities and made the assertion that there is no rule against the presentation or the introduction of two bills or two resolutions on the same subject matter. That is a correct statement based on the authorities, but I would point out that in May's fifteenth edition, at page 499 where the quotation appears, the word "presentation" is in italics. In other words, there is a distinction between being permitted

to present two resolutions or two bills dealing with the same subject and being permitted to proceed with two bills or two resolutions dealing with the same subject matter. That is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce is now asking the house to do. The house has already proceeded to a certain extent with this first resolution and he is asking, by the motion which he has now made, to proceed with the second resolution which is substantially the same as the first in that it includes everything that is in the first resolution plus some additional material.
From that point, sir, you moved on to quote a precedent which it so happens is one of the precedents upon which I rely for my side of the argument. When I quote the words of Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, I think it will be made clear that this witness is mine rather than yours. The reference you made, sir, was to the bill amending the Senate and House of Commons Act in the second session of 1945. All members who were here at that time will have vivid memories of that bill which was the one that provided for our $2,000 expense allowance. May I remind hon. members what happened. Mr. King put the resolution on the order paper quite early in the session and it remained there for quite a number of weeks. Finally, after considerable discussion mainly out of the house, the government decided to change that resolution and substitute for it a different resolution which had in it everything that was in the first resolution plus some additional material. I emphasize the fact that that is exactly what is before us now.
In 1945 there was a resolution that called for certain expenditures and a substitute resolution calling for those original expenditures plus something further. The first resolution on this matter went a certain distance and the second went that distance plus a little more. What did Mr. King, that master of parliamentary finesse, do when he had to deal with this matter in 1945? speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PROCEDURE TO BE FOLLOWED IN CONNECTION WITH STANDING ORDERS 24 AND 25
speechtext:
Earlier today the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) moved that the house do proceed to orders of the day, and later the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) attempted to move that the house do now adjourn. The first motion was moved by virtue of standing order 24 and the other by virtue of standing order 25. I think perhaps I should have listened more carefully to the intervention by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker).
I should like to say that these two motions are superseding motions; therefore a motion should have been before the house first to be superseded by the motion made by the hon. member for Kamloops. It so happens that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was allowed to make his motion to adjourn the house after the motion was moved by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the house do go into committee of the whole at its next sitting on the resolution. The motion to adjourn the house was in order.
I should like to refer hon. members to standing order 24, which says;
A motion for reading the orders of the day shall have preference to any motion before the house.
There has to be a motion before the house before that motion can be entertained. Standing order 25 says:
A motion to adjourn (except when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance), shall always be in order, but no second motion to the same effect shall be made until after some intermediate proceeding has been had.
The words "shall always be in order" must be understood to mean providing there is a motion before the house.
I should like to refer hon. members now to Bourinot's fourth edition, page 322, where he says:
There is a class of motions, common to all parliamentary assemblies, intended to have the effect of superseding or delaying the consideration of a question. For instance, motions for the adjournment of the house or debate, for reading the orders of the day, and for the previous question, are all in this direction.
The term "dilatory" is used by most writers on parliamentary law as a convenient means of grouping together such motions as postpone a question for the time being.
3768	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry
Motions of adjournment-When any question is under the consideration of either house, a motion to adjourn will always be in order.
Then he cites rule 39, which is now our rule 25. On page 324 he says:
A motion to proceed to the orders of the day is another mode of evading a question for the time being.
He cites rule 35, which is now rule 24. Then he says:
If a question on the motion paper is under consideration, any member may move, "That the orders of the day be now read," or "That the house do now proceed to the orders of the day," or "to the public bills and orders."
Now, having said that, I think we are protected for the future.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OP BRANCH LINE FROM BARTIBOG TO TOMOGONOPS RIVER, NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this bill was given careful consideration by the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. During the course of the discussion in the committee we heard evidence from Mr. S. W. Fairweather, who is the vice-president in charge of research and development for the Canadian National Railways, and because the story he told about this proposed branch line in New Brunswick was so interesting, and 1 think of such great importance to the whole of Canada, I am trespassing on the time of the committee for a few moments this afternoon to emphasize some of the statements he made.
He told us he was happier over this branch line than he had been over any other branch line of the Canadian National Railways in recent years. Then he went on to point out the significant mineral deposits that have been found in this particular part of New Brunswick. I hold in my hand the evidence taken in the committee, and at page 51 Mr. Fairweather had this to say:
The area in. New Brunswick in which the Heath Steele mine is located has developed into one of the major mineral belts of Canada.
And again, at page 56, I asked him this question:
I understood you to say that Heath Steele mines was getting established and that you expected that there would be quite a large number of mines in that area? Is that correct?
A. Yes. I am distinctly optimistic about this area. I would say that we have in this area one of the major mineral deposits in Canada. I think that is emerging. It is a zinc-lead-copper area, and the favourable area, so far as now known for prospecting would extend all the way from-let us say-a point 20 miles to the north of Newcastle up to, let us say, the vicinity of Campbellton, and halfway over to the Saint John river. It is an enormously large area, and we now know that, in addition. Heath Steele mines have proved an area of ore deposits of 7,200,000 tons of ore.
A few miles away you have the New Brunswick Mining and Smelting Corporation, and they have 50 million tons of ore that have been demonstrated: and in the same general area you have Kennco 67509-239J
Canadian National Railways mines with their prospecting, and the Texas Gulf Sulphur in prospecting, and the New Larder "U" Island mines, and while we have not shown them-
He was referring to the map which he produced in the committee.
-there are other substantial mining companies which are prospecting in the area and they are, according to my information, getting indications. Therefore I think you can say that this area is one of the prosperous spots on the mining horizon.
Q. You say that the whole area of mineral formation is lead-zinc-copper?
A. So far as is known it is zinc-lead-copper, with some gold and silver.
Then on page 57 Mr. Fairweather said:
This area has turned out in such a short period as has elapsed from the time of the first discovery-it has turned up something in the order of 60 million tons of ore, which moves this area right up into the topnotch areas of the world.
That is very significant evidence and very encouraging not only to the people of New Brunswick but also to the rest of the Canadian people because, as we all know, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island have not had the advantage of northern areas through which the great shield in Canada runs, which is so heavily mineralized; and it is almost a miracle that here in New Brunswick these vast deposits have been discovered.
I also asked Mr. Fairweather about the possibility of a smelter to fabricate those ores. The questions and answers are found on page 57. I think this particular aspect of the development is of vital importance, because someone will have to take the responsibility of aiding in the development of a smelter and a refinery, and I believe the dominion government should give a lead in that regard. I asked this question:
We hear a great deal about a smelter to be erected, and of course if that were done there would be greatly increased freight traffic, I presume. Has your company given any consideration to that possibility?
A. Oh yes, we have given a great deal of consideration to the location of a smelter. It may be recalled that when I was giving evidence on the Chibougamau line I pointed to the strategic importance of the Saguenay river, and there is now under development a smelter in that area.
This New Brunswick area is creating quite a problem because the ore is a highly complex ore. The metallurgy is very difficult. But at some stage I am hopeful that a smelter will be located and a refinery will be located, and that is probably as good a place of assured supply as any that I know of.
From a development point of view we are keenly interested in getting a customs nickle smelter-
I think that is a misprint. I think he said "zinc smelter". I continue:
-located somewhere in eastern Canada and we feel that from the development standpoint that it is a logical development. We have had talks with many industrialists and they have all agreed that at some stage we should have a zinc refinery-

Canadian National Railways
That is in addition to the smelter.
-a small refinery-in eastern Canada. It is already the hope of the chemical industry, and it is purely a matter of timing; but one of the things that has to be considered is an assured supply of zinc concentrates.
Q. You have that in this area?
A. In this area there is such an enormous amount of zinc that anybody controlling the mining here would know very definitely that for a period of a hundred years at least he would have no question at all as to the supply of zinc concentrates.
That shows just what the possibilities are arising out of those mineral discoveries. We also asked Mr. Fairweather what power would be required for the smelter. For example, I asked:
How would a smelter and a refinery derive their power? Would it be from electricity, or from coal, or from what? What would be the fuel used?
A. A smelter of course is a thermal process and it would be based largely on present knowledge, either on coal or on petroleum, one or the other, as a source of energy.
Of course that is so important because of the coal in New Brunswick and in Nova Scotia. By the way, it would not be of much help if oil were used rather than coal for fuel in such a smelter. I continue:
With a refinery, so far as zinc is concerned, you have your choice; you could either use a thermal reduction process, if you want to get high quality zinc, followed by redistillation, or you could use [DOT]electric reduction, and in the latter case of course you would have to have a cheap source of power. Speaking as a maritimer, I would be delighted if I could see a cheaper source of power developed in the maritimes than now exists.
Q. Would the development of the Saint John river mean power which was cheap enough for that purpose?

I believe he is an extremely competent and reliable official of the Canadian National Railways who is vitally interested in the development of those different Canadian resources. Here, as he said, is a branch line which has excited him more than any other. By the way, I have heard him deal with the branch lines from Terrace to Kitimat, from Sherridon to Lynn Lake, Manitoba, and then in the Chibougamau area and the branch line to lake Manitou-wadge in northern Ontario, all of which were exciting in their own right, but I feel there is an outstanding potential in this development in the province of New Brunswick. I hope the Minister of Transport or some other minister of the government will tell us whether there is in mind any policy which will promote the widest possible use of these mineral deposits for the benefit of the people of New Brunswick.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to
make a few brief remarks on the first clause of this bill. As a member of the committee on railways, canals and telegraphs who had the opportunity to hear Mr. Fairweather, who I understand is a vice-president of the Canadian National Railways connected with development and planning-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OP BRANCH LINE FROM BARTIBOG TO TOMOGONOPS RIVER, NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
I heard Mr. Fairweather
give his evidence in connection with the necessity for the building of this railway. It was most interesting for me to hear his evidence as to the great possibilities in the development of mining in New Brunswick, possibilities which apparently have come to the fore in the last three or four years, and his relation of that development to transportation necessities in the whole area and his reasons for the necessity for building this railroad to take the concentrates from the concentrator to seaboard or to other markets.
I was particularly pleased to notice his opinion that it would be necessary for a custom smelter to be built somewhere in the maritimes to serve the mines that are coming in the future. I must say I think we are very fortunate in Canada to have a gentleman

of such high capacity and vast ability as Mr. Fairweather rendering the service he does to the people of this country.
I have had the opportunity, as has the hon. member who preceded me, to hear Mr. Fair-weather give evidence on a number of occasions in connection with bills that were coming before the house, and transportation problems. It clearly indicates to me that he is an expert in his field and believes in planning. His evidence is of such a nature that one sees that he believes in relating one set of circumstances to another and acting as a result of a planned and co-ordinated approach to transportation and economic problems. We in the C.C.F. are very pleased indeed to see at least that aspect of C.C.F. policy being given effect by one of the government's most prominent servants.

subsubtopic: CONSTRUCTION OP BRANCH LINE FROM BARTIBOG TO TOMOGONOPS RIVER, NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the witness, Mr. Fairweather, in giving the information he did, was certainly most free and willing and he did not hesitate to answer any questions that were put before him. I was particularly interested in noting some of his observations with regard to the development that is expected to take place in the New Brunswick region and the part the Canadian National Railways hopes to play in it. I was somewhat disappointed, however, in the point of view the Canadian National Railways is apparently taking today in the development of such regions.
I refer specifically to what in my view should be the purpose of a railway. It should not be simply to develop an area; that is, to project a line into a particular area with the hope of making a profit, especially when it is a government-owned railway. I feel it should be for the purpose of opening up that country. As was indicated by Mr. Fair-weather, the railway may in the course of events assist other mining industries; however, the witness indicated to us in his evidence that he did not think it was up to the railway to provide bus transportation, for instance, or other means of transportation from the homes of the miners to the mine as the case might be. The purpose of this rail line was for making a profit out of the concentrates being taken from the Heath Steele mines to the main branch of the Canadian National Railways and off to Newcastle or some other port.
It is my opinion, Mr. Chairman, that while there is a road which the Heath Steele mines helped to build, it is not up to the railway to tell the mining company or the miners that those who work in the mines shall now use bus transportation which is not being provided on that road. If the rail line is going to provide cheaper transportation with respect to hauling concentrates
Canadian National Railways certainly the miners should have the right to expect that other means of transportation by rail should be offered to them as well in so far as getting to and from the mine is concerned, especially when it is considered that a good portion of the concentrates will be sent eventually to Newcastle and out through the seaport there.
The fact that the Heath Steele mine helped the province of New Brunswick build the road indicates that the mine felt some responsibility to the miners beyond getting rid of the concentrates. On page 51 of the evidence we find Mr. Fairweather's own words:
[DOT] * * we had actually to canvass this mining company and convince them that they would be better off if they were served by a railway than if they depended solely upon highway transport.
I have no objection to them making it possible for the Heath Steele mine to reduce the price of the mineral by making available to it the Canadian National Railways transportation system. However, I do object to the fact that we have here an instance wherein all the lucrative cargo is taken from the trucks and the skim or poorer part of it is passed on to a bus company which does not even exist.
When questioned concerning this point, Mr. Fairweather indicated there were automobiles that would transport people from Newcastle to the mine. It was the intention of the mine-and it is a policy that is being followed quite freely in other mining areas today-to have the miners live about 38 miles from the mine, at Newcastle or some other central point, and travel back and forth each day between Newcastle and the mine. It is possible that this in itself would be quite satisfactory, but no means is available today for those people to get back and forth, nor is it the intention of the Canadian National Railways to provide such facilities. I feel that some such means of transportation should be made available to them.
I am not suggesting for one moment that the miners would ride back and forth in the trucks that would haul the concentrates, but if the Heath Steele company felt it was necessary to assist the province of New Brunswick in building a road they would in all likelihood continue to feel a responsibility for helping to maintain that particular road. We understand that the province of New Brunswick is in need of assistance from time to time, and the assistance the Heath Steele company would give them in the building of their road would, I am sure, be very much appreciated by the people of that province. If this bill passes and this method of moving the concentrates is accepted, then these people will feel they have no obligation in respect to providing transportation back and

Canadian National Railways forth because of the lack of a road. I think our railway company should accept the responsibility in this matter.
Another matter that arose in committee had to do with agreed charges, and the witness is reported on page 51 as having said: We did a pretty fair job, and not only did we convince them that they would be better off with the railway but we also convinced them that they could afford to give us a traffic guarantee of substantial volume sufficient to lift this branch line from a speculative position to a straight business proposition.
There was a guarantee given by the mine to the C.N.R. for the building of the branch line. If they did not carry out their guarantee then I understand the mine would have to pay a penalty to the C.N.R. In other words the mine has guaranteed the C.N.R. that either it will supply sufficient concentrates to be hauled over the line to make it pay for itself within a period of ten years, or in the event of not having the concentrates to ship over the line the mine will pay a penalty. The C.N.R. lose absolutely nothing, but they are not willing to accept the responsibility of providing other means so the miners and other people in that area may travel.
Coming back to this question of agreed charges, Mr. Fairweather indicated that he did not think this was a case of agreed charges. Hon. members of the committee can read his suggestion on page 62 in respect to agreed charges, where he indicated that this was different from the agreed charges normally entered into. Technically there might be some slight difference, but certainly there is an agreement with the Steele people as to the rate they are going to be charged and the traffic load they are going to guarantee, or in the event that the guarantee is not lived up to a penalty will be paid by the Steele people. This in effect means that there are agreed charges.
What is actually going to result is that a group of truckers will be put out of business in that province, truckers who have helped to maintain the road. When we enter into such agreements I think we have a responsibility to find out how many people are going to be put out of business. If small businessmen such as these truckers are going to be put out of business we will not be helping the people there.
I know it is not the responsibility of the C.N.R. to go around and find out what people are being put out of business and then give them jobs, or something like that; but the committee should have information as to how many truckers are going to be put out of business. We have not seen the exact terms of the agreement or how much they are


being guaranteed in the way of haulage, but I can well imagine that there will be few truckers left on that road. The result will be that the province of New Brunswick will lose revenue in the form of licence fees and taxes from those particular people.

Mr. Chairman, I sat in on the committee meetings, and like other hon. members I was very interested in the evidence given by Mr. Fairweather. I find myself rather bewildered by the statements just made by the hon. member for New Westminster. If I heard him correctly, the hon. member was suggesting that truckers were going to be put out of business in the province of New Brunswick. My understanding of the evidence given to us is that the particular mine to be served by the proposed branch line is in the development stage and that some time in the future, probably a few months before it is anticipated the branch line will be constructed, they expect to begin stockpiling a certain amount of concentrates. I fail to understand the reasoning of the hon. member for New Westminster in suggesting that truckers are going to be put out of business in the hauling of concentrates that are still buried in the ground within the limits of that mining property.
There is another way in which I find myself bewildered. The hon. member seems to be concerned that the C.N.R. should be hauling people back and forth between Newcastle and the mine. If I understood Mr. Fairweather correctly he intimated that under certain terms and conditions the C.N.R. would be quite prepared to provide passenger service if there were any call for such service. According to the map shown to the committee the proposed route of this line is more or less in the shape of a dog's leg between the mining property and Newcastle, whereas the highway, which I gather is quite adequate to permit people to travel back and forth, goes along the other side of the triangle, a much shorter and more expeditious route for people to travel back and forth.
I fail to understand the reasoning of the hon. member for New Westminster. Where it is necessary and reasonable for a railway company to provide passenger service, by all means they should be prepared to do so; but under these conditions it seems to me the hon. member's argument is a little absurd.

Canadian National Railways I was taken aback-in fact, I nearly fell out of my chair-when I saw Halifax mentioned. Coming from New Brunswick and the good old port of Saint John, I realize that reference should be made to that port. When this bill was presented for second reading I had occasion to express my appreciation to the government and to the Canadian National Railways for wanting to proceed with the construction of this spur line in connection with the development of the minerals in New Brunswick. I can understand the enthusiasm which was expressed by Mr. Fairweather because it is in line with the report which was made in 1953 when the discoveries of minerals in northern New Brunswick were mentioned as the mining discovery of the year.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am not surprised to see that the members from the other end of Canada, the hon. member for New Westminster and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, are somewhat embarrassed by that situation in New Brunswick. The hon. member for New Westminster mentioned that the construction of this railway would have some effect in reducing employment for truckers and others in New Brunswick. I want to make it clear that before the mining companies approached the Canadian National Railways for the construction of this line they made a complete study of the situation. They studied the different ways of transporting minerals to the main shipping points. I have had occasion to have private discussions with certain officials of these companies, and they have been studying even the possibility of transporting minerals by air. But after careful study they decided that the cheapest, most economical way was to use the Canadian National Railways.
So far as this penalty clause is concerned, it has been mentioned as one that might restrict employment. On the contrary this penalty clause is one which means the company will have to have a certain minimum tonnage per year, and I think that will force the company to continue operations, not to curtail them, for if operations were curtailed it would also curtail employment.
Just before the recess the hon. member for Saint John-Albert expressed the opinion that the port of Halifax should not have been mentioned. I agree with him that we have in New Brunswick the port of Saint John, but we do not have to go to Saint John, which is 200 miles from the mine. Only 30 or 40 miles from these mineral deposits, we have shipping facilities just outside of Bathurst harbour. In fact last year two test pits were dredged outside the port of Bathurst as an experiment. It is proving very satisfactory. Should it be that this is not altogether satisfactory to the mines for shipping minerals out of the country after they have been processed, we have at Pokesudi, as I have mentioned previously in this house, only 60 miles from the mine, sufficient depth of water

within 200 or 300 feet from the shore to provide for deep water shipping 12 months of the year.
The hon. member for Saint John-Albert also expressed a desire to have the contract given, if possible, to a New Brunswick or maritime company. He expressed the opinion, too, that we did not have contractors able to undertake such projects. Well, I cannot agree with that statement, because in New Brunswick we have such companies as the Diamond Construction Company which already has contracts for $2 [DOT] 5 million in Halifax for the construction of an airport and contracts for over $3 million at Gagetown. We have other companies, such as Modern Construction and Dexter Construction, which could easily undertake such projects. All I would add is that if and when contracts are given by the Canadian National Railways, they should follow the policy of granting the contract to the lowest tenderer, if he is qualified to do the job, and not do as the province of New Brunswick did when the Beechwood contract was awarded.

Mr. Chairman, I really cannot leave the hon. member for Bow River under the misapprehension he has with regard to this proposed arrangement between the mining company and the Canadian National Railways. He has referred to Mr. Fairweather's evidence before the committee, and during his remarks he kept insisting on calling the arrangement an agreed charge. Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to read to this committee one of the questions the hon. member for Bow River put during the course of the proceedings before the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. On page 53 the hon. member asked the following question:
Q. You have a virtual monopoly on the freight hauled and on the passenger service as well?
A. There will be no passenger service involved in this. We made it quite plain to the company that the highway was a more efficient tool for transporting passengers than the railway; in consequence, we have no position with regard to that.
Moreover, you are in error. There is no monopoly. They do not have to ship one pound of freight over this railway-the only thing is that if they do not ship a certain volume of the production of the mine over the railway they would be obliged to pay us a penalty.
This is the significant question, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member for Bow River said:
Q. That is practically an agreed charge, is it not?
A. No, it is not an agreed charge. You could not possibly call this an agreed charge.
Now, Mr. Chairman, in the face of the evidence from someone who is in the railroad business and who knows what an agreed charge is, the hon. member has been trying to impress upon this committee the idea that the railway here is making an agreement which is tying up all the traffic from the mine. When he spoke about a percentage a little earlier I interrupted him to say there had been no question of any percentage in that. I was quite right. Ordinarily when railways do make an agreed charge there is a condition that the shippers shall give to the railways not less than a certain stated percentage of the freight which they are


shipping. The 90 per cent to which my hon friend referred a moment ago, and which is mentioned on page 59, has nothing to do with the contract. These questions were also asked by the hon. member for Bow River:
Q. You said that your outgoing traffic would be concentrates?
A. Yes.
Q. About 90 per cent?
A. Yes.
That means the concentrates represented 90 per cent of the total traffic. Well, now, that is not an agreed charge, Mr. Chairman. I hope the hon. member for Bow River will realize that what is at issue here is a traffic agreement between the Canadian National Railways and the mining company, the purpose of which is to assure the building of the line.
I explained how the traffic guarantee would operate when we were dealing with this matter at the resolution stage and on second reading. In essence what it means is this. The railroad must make an investment of approximately $3 million in order to build this line from Bartibog to the Tomogonops river, a distance of some 22 miles. It is perfectly clear from the bill and from the explanations that have been given that the cost of the work is going to be something slightly less than $3 million, and that money is going to be spent whether traffic flows over it or not.
Once the line has been built the money has been committed irrevocably; and for that reason, Mr. Chairman, it is perfectly logical that the Canadian National Railways, when requested to make an expenditure of this dimension, should say to the mining company which is quite anxious to make use of the railroad facilities-because otherwise they would never honour the agreements-"Will you guarantee to us that you will give us a minimum of 75,000 tons of concentrates each year, or if you do not that you will pay us a penalty" which I think I said the other day was $3 per ton.
I also explained that if in one year the concentrates shipped exceeded 75,000 tons, then the excess would be credited against a deficiency in any subsequent year. What surprises me, Mr. Chairman, when I hear the hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for New Westminster, is that they seem to resent the fact that the Canadian National Railways are taking what I regard as an elementary precaution to protect themselves against loss. Ordinarily the criticism is that the loss has been realized and that the railroad has not taken precautions to avoid it. This time the criticism is that we are taking precautions to avoid losses.

The hon. member for New Westminster complains that the railway company is not going to provide a passenger service; yet it is perfectly clear from the evidence before the committee-and the hon. member for New Westminster was present-that the arrangement between the railway company and the mining company expressly excluded any obligation on the part of the C.N.R. to provide passenger service. Why? I think it was the hon. member for Comox-Alberni who explained the geography. First of all it is longer by rail, and second it is much more economical to use a highway for the transport of people from Newcastle to the mine.
Hon. members will recall that Mr. Fair-weather explained, too, that it seemed desirable that the community facilities which exist at Newcastle should serve those who would find employment at the mine, and it was much more desirable that those facilities should be used than that they be duplicated by building a community at the mine site itself.
The hon. members for New Westminster and Bow River also seemed to work up a certain amount of sympathy over the situation of the truckers. Is it not elementary, Mr. Chairman, that where we are dealing with such things as concentrates, a bulk shipment, it is natural for such shipments to be carried by rail and not by road? Hon. members know perfectly well that the concentrates, as was explained before the committee, may go almost anywhere once they have been produced; they will probably be sold and they may go overseas, to the United States or to some other part of Canada. They are not, however, going to be carried overseas by trucks, nor are they going to be carried to the United States by trucks.
The next point is that all the sympathy that is being worked up relates to truckers who do not yet exist, because there have been no shipments out of the mine. The hon. member for New Westminster was shedding tears over the unfortunate plight of those truckers who might carry the concentrates if the company decided to ship them by truck. Well, Mr. Chairman, I am not ready to join in shedding tears over people who do not already have the business. If the railways were taking it away from them I would have a certain amount of sympathy, but not too much. Here is something that properly belongs to the railways. I do not think my hon. friends should shed too many tears over these mythical truckers who so far have not carried a ton of concentrates.
In essence, Mr. Chairman, this is a very simple transaction. Canadian National Railways is proposing to spend approximately $3
Canadian National Railways million to bring rail facilities into the heart of an area which seems most promising so far as base metals are concerned. We know how easy it is for truckers to pull up, move their trucks and go elsewhere, but we all should realize it is not possible for the railway to do the same thing. Once the line goes down it would take a great deal of time and effort to get it up, and there naturally would be a great deal of capital lost in the process.
It is for that reason the railways wish to insure themselves against loss by saying to the mining company, "If you wish to have our services and if you are going to be our principal client, then guarantee that you will give us the traffic". If the mining company does not wish to give the railway the traffic and wishes instead to ship by some other means it is perfectly free to do so, but it must make good on the guarantee which they have given to the railway and which is the reason the railway is going to spend approximately $3 million for the building of this line.
There is only one other observation I should like to make, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra seemed to think this was a good opportunity to get in a crack in favour of the dominion government giving the lead in the building of a customs smelter. Well, Mr. Chairman, I know that the words, "Giving the lead" are open to a very wide variety of interpretations. I can just imagine how the hon. member would lift his hands in horror if it were to be suggested that the dominion government was going to finance such a project as that-

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at ten o'clock last Thursday I was in the process of pointing out some inadequacies in the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I had said that in my opinion the act seemed to be moving backwards instead of forward. I had drawn attention to the fact that I had placed on the order paper at the beginning of this session a resolution which had I had the opportunity to move it would have called for a considerable widening of the operations of that act.
In recent months there have been two events which have caused considerable anxiety in the prairie provinces, particularly in Manitoba, with respect to the small projects or special votes under the act. I had mentioned that one of the arrangements under which a certain number of special projects had been constructed in Manitoba was an agreement between the federal government and the province, involving also the municipalities, under which the federal government paid approximately 50 per cent of the cost while the province shared the other 50 per cent with the municipalities.
While those conditions were appreciated as being better than nothing we found that in many cases, because the full project hinged upon the ability of the local municipality to pay its share of the cost, which ran in the neighbourhood of one-sixth plus the right of way, those municipalities which most needed the drainage or flood control projects were least able to meet the cost. For that reason, in many cases where these flood control measures were required they were not carried out because, as I said, the first move had to be up to the municipality.
Since that time two things have happened that have caused concern in Manitoba. Earlier this year-I think I mentioned this in the house before-the Minister of Agriculture had notified the provincial minister of agriculture in Manitoba that when the provincial government wishes to have a survey made in order to establish the feasability of a particular project with regard to flood control, whereas in the past the federal government was willing to lend the services of the P.F.R.A. engineers at their own cost, in future the province would have to pay for any such survey out of their own treasury.

Supply-Agriculture
That in itself, in my opinion, was instrumental in holding back a number of surveys the provincial government would like to have had carried out.
Later on this year there was another change made in the arrangements, and that involved the sharing of the cost. I have also already described this. Under a special vote the federal government was prepared to pay 50 per cent of the cost of these small projects. Later on the federal government took the position that any future joint undertakings of that nature would be carried out under the water conservation act rather than under a special vote of the P.F.R.A.
I have in my hand a clipping from the Winnipeg Free Press dated March 7, 1956, which I think indicates how widespread the concern was in that province. In fairly bold headlines the news item reads as follows:
Ottawa Chops Aid In Flood Projects
It then goes on to describe what had happened in these words:
Ottawa has blasted Manitoba hopes for a possible 100 per cent federal payment on large flood protection projects in this province.
Speaking in the legislature Tuesday night, Premier D. L. Campbell said he understood that in future flood protection and remedial projects would come under provisions of the water conservation assistance act-rather than under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
Further down in this news item it describes what the effect of this new policy would be, in these words:
This would cut federal aid by 60 per cent in some cases.
Under the water conservation act, the federal and provincial government each pay 37i per cent of the cost for projects approved by both parties. The other 25 per cent would be levied against municipalities.
May I just pause there to point out that if this policy is carried out it will be adding a further burden to the municipalities, which already in many cases were not capable of carrying even one-sixth of the cost of these projects, which were very necessary in our province. If this policy is carried through they will be asked to contribute 25 per cent instead of approximately 16 per cent, as was the case before. The news item goes on further in these words:
The change has dealt a serious blow to Manitoba's hopes to ^ have P.F.R.A. undertake at least two large projects, the widening and controlling of the Fairford river channel, leading from lake Manitoba to lake Winnipeg, and some work on flood protection for the Red river valley.
Then it goes on in greater detail. Just in case the Minister of Agriculture might think this is only the view of one of the newspapers of my province-

I rise on a point of order. The fact is that these particular works of

If that is the case then certainly the minister of agriculture in the province of Manitoba should be so informed, because I was just about to place on the record the comments that minister made with regard to the very things of which I am talking. Manitoba's agriculture minister Hon. R. D. Robertson, Wednesday expressed dissatisfaction of federal government failure to implement a single flood control and soil conservation policy for Canada, or at least for the prairie provinces.
At the same time, he said he was "displeased" over the dominion's new water control formula, under which Ottawa and the province bear equal shares of 75 per cent of the cost of such measures, with municipalities absorbing the remaining 25 per cent.
The minister may say that the water conservation act does not have any direct connection with the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, or that these special projects do not come within the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and he may be technically correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture

Mr. Chairman, I shall be very glad to follow your suggestion. I shall not need to review what I have already said, but I think we can agree on this much with the Minister of Agriculture, that as he has himself stated just a few minutes ago, certain arrangements have been made between his department and the department of agriculture in the province of Manitoba. Certainly those arrangements must concern the administration of the Department of Agriculture here, and, to the extent they do, I submit that certainly it is in order to discuss those arrangements. I shall refrain from any further reference to the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act until we come to that particular item, if that is more convenient.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We had better get it all understood to begin with. My hon. friend was speaking of the connection between lake Manitoba and lake Winnipeg. That is not in the P.F.R.A. area, and we have no arrangements whatsoever with regard to that. P.F.R.A. does not take care of flood conditions around those lakes.
